records.text: The nickel-chelation study by Benoit and colleagues tested dimethylglyoxime, abbreviated DMG, rather than EDTA. Its introduction distinguishes this nickel-preferring compound from older chelators. Findings about a named chelator therefore need to remain attached to that compound rather than being treated as interchangeable evidence for EDTA.
records.publicSuffix: (Source locator: PDF p1 Abstract; p2 Introduction). [[benoit-2019-nickel-chelation-therapy-mdr-enteric-pathogens]]

records.text: The reported experiments include bacterial cultures, infected mice and wax-moth larvae. Enzyme activity, bacterial growth and animal infection outcomes are different endpoints. These experiments provide preclinical context for metal sequestration; they do not establish the safety or effectiveness of an EDTA treatment regimen in people.
records.locator: PDF p1 Abstract; p8 Galleria experiments
records.publicSuffix: (Source locator: PDF p1 Abstract; p8 Galleria experiments). [[benoit-2019-nickel-chelation-therapy-mdr-enteric-pathogens]]

records.text: The environmental review by Briffa and colleagues separates human activities such as mining, industry and agriculture from natural processes such as weathering and volcanic activity. These are descriptions of potential exposure sources, rather than measurements of the exposure received by a particular person.
records.publicSuffix: (Source locator: PDF p2 Sections 2 and 3). [[briffa-2020-heavy-metal-pollution-environment-toxicology]]

records.text: The same review distinguishes ingestion, inhalation and skin contact as routes by which metals can enter the body. Keeping the route and chemical form visible helps distinguish environmental occurrence from internal exposure. A list of possible sources is not a reconstructed lifetime exposure history.
records.publicSuffix: (Source locator: PDF p2 Section 3). [[briffa-2020-heavy-metal-pollution-environment-toxicology]]

records.text: Luqman and colleagues review links between the intestinal microbiome, microbial metabolites and cardiovascular risk factors, including inflammation and diabetes. This is a synthesis of existing literature, rather than a newly recruited cohort in which all of those conditions were measured together.
records.publicSuffix: (Source locator: PDF p1 Abstract; p2 Introduction). [[luqman-2024-intestinal-microbiome-cvd-intervention]]

records.text: The review discusses short-chain fatty acids, bile acids and trimethylamine-related metabolism as possible connections between intestinal and cardiovascular biology. A shared pathway can motivate investigation of comorbidity, but the review does not establish that every person with overlapping diagnoses has the same microbial cause.
records.publicSuffix: (Source locator: PDF p1 Abstract; p2 Introduction). [[luqman-2024-intestinal-microbiome-cvd-intervention]]

records.text: The vaginal microbiome study by Yang and colleagues compares microbial composition and function in HPV16-positive and control samples using shotgun metagenomics, with selected markers assessed separately by quantitative PCR. These are measurements of community composition and gene markers, rather than a direct map of an intestinal oxygen gradient.
records.locator: PDF p1 Abstract; p2 Study Population and Sampling
records.publicSuffix: (Source locator: PDF p1 Abstract; p2 Study Population and Sampling). [[yang-2020-vaginal-microbiome-hpv16-shotgun-metagenomics]]

records.text: The authors describe host characteristics, personal hygiene, sexual behavior and hormonal cycling as potential confounders. They also state that their cross-sectional study cannot determine which condition preceded the other. An association between infection and microbial composition therefore needs to remain distinct from an established oxygen-driven causal sequence.
records.publicSuffix: (Source locator: PDF p12 Discussion and limitations). [[yang-2020-vaginal-microbiome-hpv16-shotgun-metagenomics]]

records.text: Duan and colleagues discuss oxalate as a microbial energy substrate and as a molecule capable of forming an insoluble complex with lead. Their review presents this as a possible connection between microbial metabolism and metal absorption, rather than a clinical trial of an oxalate-based intervention.
records.publicSuffix: (Source locator: PDF p3 Section 2.1). [[duan-2020-gut-microbiota-heavy-metal-probiotic-strategy]]

records.text: The review also separates microbial binding and transformation of metals from experiments using antibiotic-treated or germ-free animals. It notes that differences in microbiota between species matter for oral metal exposure. Those animal and chemical observations cannot simply be read as a demonstrated treatment effect in humans.
records.publicSuffix: (Source locator: PDF p3 Section 2.1). [[duan-2020-gut-microbiota-heavy-metal-probiotic-strategy]]

records.text: Aquino and colleagues examine epidemiological, animal and cell studies when assessing the metalloestrogen hypothesis. Their review emphasizes that metal concentration and binding to proteins other than estrogen receptors complicate interpretation. A cellular estrogen-like response is therefore not interchangeable with evidence of cancer development in a population.
records.publicSuffix: (Source locator: PDF p1 Abstract). [[aquino-2012-cadmium-nickel-metalloestrogens]]

records.text: The authors explicitly describe uncertainty about whether chronic, low-level cadmium or nickel exposure directly causes cancer development and progression. The term metalloestrogen identifies a proposed mode of action under investigation; it does not remove the need to distinguish exposure, receptor signaling and clinical disease.
records.publicSuffix: (Source locator: PDF p1 Abstract; p2 Introduction). [[aquino-2012-cadmium-nickel-metalloestrogens]]

records.text: Robinson and Glasfeld discuss the binding series in the setting of nascent protein sites with little steric selection. Their commentary explains that cells also control metal bioavailability, so the metal that binds most tightly in a simplified comparison need not be the metal delivered to a protein inside a cell.
records.locator: PDF p1 Abstract and opening discussion
records.publicSuffix: (Source locator: PDF p1 Abstract and opening discussion). [[robinson-2020-metalation-natures-challenge]]

records.text: The commentary describes how linked metal-binding sites, changes in coordination geometry and accessory processes can alter selectivity. It specifically allows binding preferences that depart from the simple series. This is why a general affinity ordering should not be treated as an exceptionless prediction for every protein or ligand.
records.publicSuffix: (Source locator: PDF p2 Discussion following Figure 1). [[robinson-2020-metalation-natures-challenge]]

records.text: The metabolomics review by Akash and colleagues emphasizes that the specimen matters: blood, urine and other samples can contain different metabolite profiles. Collection, storage, extraction and analytical platform also affect the result. A biomarker description therefore needs to identify what was measured and how it was measured.
records.locator: PDF p2 Section 2; p3 workflow discussion
records.publicSuffix: (Source locator: PDF p2 Section 2; p3 workflow discussion). [[akash-2023-metabolomics-heavy-metal-toxicities]]

records.text: The authors call for reproducible workflows and further validation of putative metabolomic biomarkers in larger cohorts. They also note potential bias and variability from laboratory models and small cohorts. Discovery of a candidate signal is a separate step from establishing a reliable clinical test.
records.publicSuffix: (Source locator: PDF p3 workflow discussion). [[akash-2023-metabolomics-heavy-metal-toxicities]]

records.text: The held Research Square preprint by Haddad and colleagues compares adults with rheumatoid arthritis, adults with fibromyalgia and healthy controls. It reports serum metal measurements alongside vitamin D and parathyroid hormone. This is a case-controlled comparison, rather than an experiment that assigns metal exposure or a treatment.
records.locator: PDF p1 preprint identity; p2 Abstract Methods
records.publicSuffix: (Source locator: PDF p1 preprint identity; p2 Abstract Methods). [[haddad-2024-heavy-metals-vitamin-d-pth-ra-fibromyalgia]]

records.text: The preprint reports correlations and proposes an explanation involving vitamin D and parathyroid hormone. Those observations do not by themselves establish the sequence of events or show that removing an exposure would correct the hormone disturbance. Its preprint status remains explicit; no peer-review approval is claimed here.
records.locator: PDF p1 preprint identity; p2 Abstract Results and Conclusion
records.publicSuffix: (Source locator: PDF p1 preprint identity; p2 Abstract Results and Conclusion). [[haddad-2024-heavy-metals-vitamin-d-pth-ra-fibromyalgia]]

records.text: Bao and colleagues distinguish storage of iron in intestinal-cell ferritin from export of iron into the circulation. Their review describes retention and eventual loss with cell shedding when cellular iron is high, and transport into the circulation when cellular iron is low. Storage and transport are separate parts of the same regulatory system.
records.publicSuffix: (Source locator: PDF p7 Section 6.1). [[bao-2024-iron-homeostasis-intestinal-immunity-gut-microbiota]]

records.text: The review places ferritin within a broader account of iron regulation involving hepcidin, iron transporters and inflammation. This mechanistic context does not turn a ferritin measurement alone into a complete explanation of iron distribution, inflammatory status or a microbiome change in an individual patient.
records.locator: PDF p5 Section 3.2; p7 opening paragraph
records.publicSuffix: (Source locator: PDF p5 Section 3.2; p7 opening paragraph). [[bao-2024-iron-homeostasis-intestinal-immunity-gut-microbiota]]

existingNarrowing.oldExact: This series holds for virtually all ligands and biological chelators. It means that copper binds more tightly than any other first-row transition metal to any given protein or small molecule, followed by zinc, then nickel, and so on. This thermodynamic reality is the reason life had to evolve elaborate metal homeostasis systems -- and why those systems are vulnerable to disruption.
existingNarrowing.newExact: The binding series is a useful starting point for understanding metal selection, but intracellular availability and the structure of a binding site also matter. Robinson and Glasfeld describe mechanisms that can produce departures from the series, rather than an exceptionless rule for every protein and ligand. (Source locator: PDF p1 opening discussion; p2 discussion following Figure 1). [[robinson-2020-metalation-natures-challenge]]
existingNarrowing.locator: PDF p1 opening discussion; p2 discussion following Figure 1
existingNarrowing.reason: Original commentary explicitly allows departures from the series; avoid retaining the unsupported universal-ligand claim.
